Proposition 1 (Closed-form Formula of the Optimal Velocity). When p_data is replaced by p_hat_data, the optimal velocity field u_hat* is given by a normalized weighted average: u_hat*(x,t) = [sum_i exp(-||x - t x^(i)||^2 / (2(1-t)^2)) (x^(i) - x)/(1-t)] / [sum_i exp(-||x - t x^(i)||^2 / (2(1-t)^2))]. snippets.location: 3 Investigating the key sources of generalization
snippets.content: Figure 1: We challenge the hypothesis that target stochasticity plays a major role in flow matching generalization. In Figure 1a, the histograms of the cosine similarities between u_hat*((1-t)x0+tx1, t) and u^cond((1-t)x0+tx1, z=x1, t)=x1-x0 are displayed for various time values t and two datasets. For real, high-dimensional data, non-stochasticity arises very early (before t=0.2 for CIFAR-10 with dimension (3,32,32)). Figure 1c displays the alignment between u_hat* and u^cond over time for varying image dimensions d on Imagenette. (a) Non-stochasticity of u_hat* for high-dimensional real data. (b) Stochasticity vs. non-stochasticity. (c) Dimension dependence.

Right: average distance between the generated samples and their closest image from the training set (horizontal dashed line = mean distance between an image of CIFAR-10 train and its nearest neighbor). All quantities are computed/learned on a varying number of training samples (10 to 10^4).

Figure 3: Generalization occurs at small times on CIFAR-10 (left) and CelebA-64 (right). Top: Generalization (distance between generated samples and training data) of hybrid models that follow u_hat* on [0, tau], then u_theta on [tau, 1]. The four colored curves correspond to four specific x0; the black dashed curve is the mean distance over the 256 generated images. Bottom: visualization of generated images for the four different starting noises and various values of tau. Following u_hat* until tau >= 0.3 yields a model that is not able to generalize.

Figure 4: FID computed on the training set (50k) and the test set (10k) using multiple embeddings, Inception and DINOv2. Regressing against a more deterministic target (EFM-128, 256, 1000) does not lead to performance decreases. On the contrary, the more deterministic the target, the better the performance. Legend: EFM-256, EFM-128, CFM, OTCFM, EFM-1000.

Algorithm 1: Vanilla Flow Matching. for k in 1..niter: t~U([0,1]); x0~N(0,Id), x1~p_hat_data; x_t=(1-t)x0+t x1; u^cond(x_t,t)=(x1-x_t)/(1-t)=x1-x0; L(theta)=||u_theta(x_t,t)-u^cond(x_t,t)||^2; update theta. return u_theta.

Algorithm 2: Empirical Flow Matching. param M. for k in 1..niter: x0~N(0,Id), x1~p_hat_data, t~U([0,1]); x_t=(1-t)x0+t x1; b^(1)=x1; for j in 2..M: b^(j)~p_hat_data; w_j=softmax_j(-||x_t - t b^(j)||^2/(2(1-t)^2)); u_hat*_M(x_t,t)=sum_j (b^(j)-x_t)/(1-t) w_j; L(theta)=||u_theta(x_t,t)-u_hat*_M(x_t,t)||^2; update theta. return u_theta.
